lines: Here is something strange about being human.
Most animals live in the world in front of them. You can sit perfectly still and rehearse a conversation that will not happen for three weeks.
With a person who has not yet said any of their lines. And who, in your head, is being quite rude.
That ability is called prospection. It is one of the most remarkable things a brain does, and one of the most error prone.
This film is about how it works, where it goes wrong, and how to use it more kindly.
The first film was about the past. This one is about the future.

Psychologists Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson put it simply. All animals can predict the consequences of things they have experienced before. Humans can predict the consequences of things they have never experienced, by simulating them in the mind.
How? In large part, by borrowing the machinery of memory.
People with damage to the hippocampus struggle to imagine new scenes, and similar brain regions are active when we recall the past and picture the future.
Your brain is a remix artist. The future is built out of pieces of your past, rearranged.
Which means your imagined tomorrow is made of yesterday, and will only be as good as the pieces on the shelf.
So how good are these simulations at predicting how we will feel? Here is the humbling part.
In studies led by Daniel Gilbert, people predicted how long they would feel bad after a breakup, an election loss, or being denied tenure. They consistently overestimated how long it would hurt.
The reason is that we do not notice our own psychological immune system, the quiet mental processes that make sense of bad news and soften it.
You have an excellent emotional immune system, and almost no idea that you have it.
Another trap is called focalism. When we imagine one event, we picture it alone. We forget that life will keep happening around it.
In one study, football fans who first thought about everything else they would be doing that week were less likely to overpredict how long a loss would affect their happiness.
Here is my favorite example.
Students in the Midwest and in Southern California rated their life satisfaction. The two groups were equally satisfied.
But when asked to guess how satisfied a similar person in the other region would be, everyone expected Californians to be happier.
The reason is the focusing illusion. We give too much weight to vivid, easy differences, like weather, and too little to the fact that real life is mostly ordinary days.
Daniel Kahneman put it this way: nothing in life is as important as you think it is, while you are thinking about it.
Which is good news if you are dreading something, and a gentle warning if you are chasing something.
Then there is the planning fallacy.
In studies by Roger Buehler and colleagues, people predicted their own task completion times too optimistically, across a variety of tasks.
Not because they lacked experience. When making predictions, they pictured the plan going smoothly, and did not consult what had happened last time.
Observers did the opposite. They overestimated how long other people would take. We are generous planners for ourselves, and strict ones for everyone else.
The fix is wonderfully unglamorous. When people were asked to connect their predictions to relevant past experiences, the optimistic bias disappeared.
So the next time you say it will take an afternoon, ask your past self. They have been waiting to be consulted.
Now, the future also visits us as worry.
In one study, people with generalized anxiety disorder wrote down their worries as they came, then checked later what had actually happened.
Ninety one percent of the worries did not come true.
In a later trial, close to nine in ten again did not. And when a feared thing did happen, people coped better than they had expected, most of the time.
Seneca said it nearly two thousand years ago: we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
This is not an instruction to stop worrying. Worry is your brain trying to protect you, like a smoke alarm that cannot tell toast from fire.
But keeping a small worry diary, and checking back, can be a surprisingly kind experiment. And if worry is heavy, a good therapist is a very good idea.
Here is a twist that surprises many people. Not every kind of positive thinking helps.

Gabriele Oettingen found that people who vividly fantasized about a wished-for future, a job, a crush, an exam, tended to put in less effort and do worse. People who simply expected good outcomes put in more.
Daydreaming about the finish line feels like progress. Your body agrees, and takes a nap.
The remedy is called mental contrasting. Picture the wish, then honestly picture the obstacle standing in the way, and let the two meet.
Then make a small if-then plan. If it is seven thirty and the kettle is on, then I write for ten minutes.
Across ninety four tests, plans like this had a medium to large effect on reaching goals. Not magic, but one of the most reliable tools we have.
One more strange fact. To your brain, your future self can feel a bit like a stranger.

In experiments by Emily Pronin and colleagues, people decided how much of a disgusting drink to take for science. They were willing to sign their future selves up for more of it than their present selves, much as they would for other people.
In other studies, Hal Hershfield and colleagues had people meet an age progressed version of themselves in virtual reality. Afterward, they were more willing to wait for larger, later rewards.

In a real world test with nearly fifty thousand savers, a similar trick helped, modestly. Contributions rose from one point five percent of people to one point seven. Small, but it cost almost nothing.
So here is a gentle practice. Treat your future self like someone you love and have not met yet. Leave them a clean kitchen. Leave them a note.
Put it together, and a picture appears.
The future is not a place you are traveling to. It is a story your brain is telling right now, built from your past, colored by your mood, and usually a little off.
Saint Augustine wrote that the present of things future is expectation. The future only ever exists as something you are doing today.

So here are four gentle questions to carry with you. What else will be happening in my life that week? How long did this take last time? If it goes badly, what will I do? And what would I say to a friend who was worried about this?
None of them predict the future. They just make the story a little kinder, and a little more accurate.
You will never arrive in the future. You will only ever arrive in the next now.
So the best thing you can do for tomorrow is to be kind to the person who is about to live it, which is you, today.
In the next film, we look at the only place where any of this happens: the present moment.
Thank you for watching.
